steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Intro
  - maps universe of keys to indices / slots in the table
  - conventional implementations: integer universe assumption (all elements stem from the universe; bit length within the word size of the computer architecture)
  - perfect for a given set = injective on it, each element maps to a different value
  - perfect hash function can be created if all keys known ahead of time
## Integer universe assumption
  - schemes: hashing by division, hashing by multiplication, universal hashing, dynamic perfect hashing, static perfect hashing
  - hashing by division is the commonly used one
## Hashing by division
  - scheme: hash value of a key, using the size of the table
## Hashing by multiplication
  - scheme uses a non-integer real-valued constant and the size of the table
  - advantage: the value is not critical
  - any value works; Donald Knuth suggests the golden ratio
## String hashing
  - strings commonly used as keys
  - The C++ Programming Language, third edition: unsigned integer starting at zero, left shift one bit, xor with next character's integer value; then modulo table size
  - non-circular left shift -> string length at least eight bits less than size of the unsigned integer in bits
  - other common way: polynomial rolling hash
## Choosing a hash function
  - uniform distribution of hash values = fundamental requirement
  - non-uniform -> more collisions, higher cost of resolving them
  - hard to ensure by design; evaluate empirically with statistical tests, e.g. Pearson's chi-squared test for discrete uniform distributions
  - only needs uniformity for table sizes occurring in the application
  - dynamic resizing with exact doubling and halving -> uniform only for power-of-two sizes; index = range of bits of the hash
  - some algorithms prefer a prime size
  - open addressing: avoid runs (two or more keys to consecutive slots); lookup cost can skyrocket even with low load factor, rare collisions
  - popular multiplicative hash claimed to have particularly poor run behavior
  - K-independent hashing: prove no bad keysets for a given type of hashtable
  - K-independence results known for linear probing, cuckoo hashing
  - once proven to work, focus on fastest such hash function

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
A hash function maps the universe of keys to indices or slots within the table, that is, for. Conventional implementations of hash functions are based on the integer universe assumption, which is that all elements of the table come from the universe, where the bit length of is confined within the word size of a computer architecture.

A hash function is perfect for a given set if it is injective on, that is, if each element maps to a different value in. If all the keys are known ahead of time, a perfect hash function can be created.

## Integer universe assumption

There are several schemes of hashing that are used in the integer universe assumption: hashing by division, hashing by multiplication, universal hashing, dynamic perfect hashing, and static perfect hashing. But hashing by division is the scheme that is commonly used.

## Hashing by division

In hashing by division the scheme is as follows: where is the hash value of and is the size of the table.

## Hashing by multiplication

In hashing by multiplication the scheme is as follows: Where is a non-integer real-valued constant and is the size of the table. One advantage of hashing by multiplication is that the is not critical. Any value produces a hash function, but Donald Knuth suggests using the golden ratio.

## String hashing

A string is commonly used as the key to the hash function. The third edition of The C++ Programming Language describes a simple hash function where an unsigned integer starts at zero and it is repeatedly left shifted one bit and then xor'ed with the integer value of the next character. Then this hash value is taken modulo the table size. If the left shift is not circular, then the string length should be at least eight bits less than the size of the unsigned integer in bits. A polynomial rolling hash function is another common way to hash a string to an integer.

## Choosing a hash function

A fundamental requirement of a hash function is that the hash values have a uniform distribution. If the distribution is non-uniform, the number of collisions goes up, and the cost of resolving them goes up too. It is sometimes difficult to ensure uniformity by design, but it can be evaluated empirically with statistical tests, e.g., a Pearson's chi-squared test for discrete uniform distributions.

The distribution only needs to be uniform for the table sizes that occur in the application. For example, if dynamic resizing is used with exact doubling and halving of the table size, the hash function only needs to be uniform when the size is a power of two. In this case the index can be computed as some range of bits of the hash function. But some hashing algorithms prefer the size to be a prime number.

For open addressing schemes the hash function should also avoid runs, which is when two or more keys are mapped to consecutive slots. Runs like this may make the lookup cost skyrocket, even when the load factor is low and collisions are infrequent. The popular multiplicative hash is claimed to have particularly poor run behavior.

K-independent hashing gives a way to prove that a certain hash function does not have bad keysets for a given type of hashtable. A number of K-independence results are known for collision resolution schemes like linear probing and cuckoo hashing. Since K-independence can prove that a hash function works, one can then focus on finding the fastest possible such hash function.
